A Systematic Review ABSTRACT The number of newborns with neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome is alarming, due to the increase in maternal opioid use. Despite the critical health and socio‐economic impact, a precise clinical and therapeutic approach for opioid using infants and mothers remains undefined. Aim The main objective is to update the therapeutic approach and the role of nursing in neonates with neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome due to mothers who use opioids. Design We conducted a systematic review, as a meta‐analysis was not feasible due to heterogeneity across study designs and outcomes, in accordance with PRISMA guidelines and the Cochrane Handbook. Methods Studies related to the update of the therapeutic approach and the role of nursing in a newborn with neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome were considered. Single patient case studies, studies of psychoactive substances other than opium derivatives, iatrogenic treatment approach, guidelines, consensus and meeting abstracts were excluded. The databases Scopus, Dialnet, Cinahl and PubMed were searched. Results The results of the 28 publications included indicated the need for a major update of both treatment, diagnostic scales and treatment in neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome. Conclusions Clonidine and buprenorphine demonstrated superior safety profiles and shorter treatment duration compared to morphine in controlling NOWS symptoms. The ESC functional assessment model, integrated with non‐pharmacological interventions, proved superior to traditional Finnegan scoring, significantly reducing pharmacotherapy requirements, total morphine exposure, hospital length of stay, and healthcare costs whilst enhancing breastfeeding rates and parental involvement. Nursing‐led holistic care, encompassing skin‐to‐skin contact, breastfeeding support, rooming‐in, and environmental control, is essential and irreplaceable in comprehensive NOWS management. Based on the above, this paper will focus exclusively on the neonatal abstinence syndrome produced by maternal consumption of opium derivatives. Neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome has become a global public health concern, with increasing incidence reported not only in North America but also in Europe, Oceania and several low‐ and middle‐income countries. In Europe, population‐based studies have reported rising rates of NOWS, particularly in countries with increased opioid prescription and opioid use disorder among women of reproductive age. Similarly, data from Australia and New Zealand show a steady increase in hospital admissions related to NOWS over the last decade. In this context, and despite the growing impact of NOWS, the health emergency and the socio‐economic crisis that opioid use is causing, the clinical and therapeutic approach in newborns opioid exposed and opioid who using mothers has not been precisely determined [2]. Opioid use constitutes not only a public health problem but also a large‐scale socioeconomic crisis. The sustained increase in opioid consumption has been associated with higher mortality rates, overburdened healthcare systems, and substantial economic costs due to lost labor productivity and increased social service needs. In the United States alone, the illicit opioid epidemic was estimated to cost the economy approximately $2.7 trillion in 2023, encompassing losses from deaths, reduced quality of life, healthcare expenses, and crime‐related costs, highlighting how opioid misuse contributes to broader social and economic harm beyond clinical outcomes [3]. fetched_contents.text: Buprenorphine for the Treatment of the Neonatal Abstinence Syndrome Abstract Background Current pharmacologic treatment of the neonatal abstinence syndrome with morphine is associated with a lengthy duration of therapy and hospitalization. Buprenorphine may be more effective than morphine for this indication. Methods In this single-site, double-blind, double-dummy clinical trial, we randomly assigned 63 term infants (≥37 weeks of gestation) who had been exposed to opioids in utero and who had signs of the neonatal abstinence syndrome to receive either sublingual buprenorphine or oral morphine. Infants with symptoms that were not controlled with the maximum dose of opioid were treated with adjunctive phenobarbital. The primary end point was the duration of treatment for symptoms of neonatal opioid withdrawal. Secondary clinical end points were the length of hospital stay, the percentage of infants who required supplemental treatment with phenobarbital, and safety. Results The median duration of treatment was significantly shorter with buprenorphine than with morphine (15 days vs. 28 days), as was the median length of hospital stay (21 days vs. 33 days) (P<0.001 for both comparisons). Adjunctive phenobarbital was administered in 5 of 33 infants (15%) in the buprenorphine group and in 7 of 30 infants (23%) in the morphine group (P=0.36). Rates of adverse events were similar in the two groups. Conclusions Among infants with the neonatal abstinence syndrome, treatment with sublingual buprenorphine resulted in a shorter duration of treatment and shorter length of hospital stay than treatment with oral morphine, with similar rates of adverse events. (Funded by the National Institute on Drug Abuse; BBORN ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT01452789.) The neonatal abstinence syndrome is defined as the occurrence of signs and symptoms of neonatal withdrawal after in utero drug exposure.1 Among drug exposures, opioids cause severe symptoms, including autonomic instability, tremor, irritability, poor feeding, and loose stool. Measures that improve symptom control include minimization of stimulation, rooming in,2 breast-feeding,3 and frequent calorically dense feedings. Approximately two thirds of infants with this condition do not have a response to behavioral approaches and ultimately require pharmacologic therapy for control of symptoms.4 The administration of an opioid at an appropriate dose for symptom control with subsequent weaning has been identified as an effective approach, but data are limited to guide the choice of opioid.5 Morphine is used in more than 80% of the infants who require treatment for the neonatal abstinence syndrome in the United States.4 In adults, sublingual buprenorphine is used to reduce symptoms of opioid withdrawal.6 Buprenorphine has a wide therapeutic index for respiratory depression and a long half-life that may make it useful for treatment of the neonatal abstinence syndrome. Open-label investigations have established a pharmacokinetic profile in neonates7 and suggested favorable safety and efficacy for this indication.8,9 In the single-site, randomized, double-blind, double-dummy Blinded Buprenorphine or Neonatal Morphine Solution (BBORN) trial, we compared sublingual buprenorphine with oral morphine with respect to the duration of treatment in infants with the neonatal abstinence syndrome. Methods Trial Design and Population From October 31, 2011, to May 29, 2016, we enrolled term infants (≥37 weeks of gestation) who had been exposed to opioids in utero and had signs and symptoms of the neonatal abstinence syndrome. Exclusion criteria were a major congenital malformation, a birth weight of less than 2200 g, a serious medical or neurologic illness, hypoglycemia requiring intravenous glucose, a bilirubin level of more than 20 mg per deciliter (342 μmol per liter), maternal use of a benzodiazepine 30 days before birth, or seizures. Breast-feeding was an exclusionary criterion until the approval of a protocol amendment on October 17, 2013. This expansion was driven by changing local and national4 practice patterns during the trial, which increased the number of women who attempted to breast-feed. Written informed consent was obtained from the parents. The trial was approved by the institutional review board at Thomas Jefferson University. The drug manufacturer, Indivior, donated the buprenorphine that was used in the trial but was not involved in the trial design, in the collection, analysis, or interpretation of the data, or in the preparation of the manuscript. The protocol, which includes the statistical analysis plan, is available with the full text of this article at NEJM.org. Published in final edited form as: Clin Pharmacol Ther. 2017 Nov 28;103(1):112–119. doi: 10.1002/cpt.930 Abstract Infants exposed in utero to opioids will demonstrate a withdrawal syndrome known as neonatal abstinence syndrome (NAS). Buprenorphine is a long-acting opioid with therapeutic use in medication-assisted treatment of opioid dependency in adults and adolescents. Emerging data from clinical trials and treatment cohorts demonstrate the efficacy and safety of sublingual buprenorphine for those infants with NAS who require pharmacologic treatment. Pharmacometric modeling will assist in defining the exposure–response relationships and facilitate dose optimization. NEONATAL ABSTINENCE SYNDROME The placental transfer of drugs from the mother to the fetus is well described. The developmental kinetics of drug permeability at the fetal “blood–brain barrier” in humans is not fully defined, but is clearly immature early in pregnancy.1 Many prescribed medications or drugs of abuse can impact postnatal outcomes, particularly with chronic use during pregnancy. Some substances cause neonatal symptomatology that is a direct effect of maternal transfer of the xenobiotic to the neonate. This is characteristic of a toxidrome. For example, intrauterine cocaine exposure is associated with tremors, high-pitched cry, and autonomic instability in the infant that is self-limited and improves as the drug is cleared from the system.2 Other psychoactive agents are associated with symptoms that emerge as the drug concentration falls within the neonate, indicating a withdrawal syndrome. Opioids, serotonin reuptake inhibitors,3 nicotine,4 and antipsychotics5 all can cause withdrawal or adaptation symptoms. The term “neonatal abstinence syndrome” is nonspecific. While the bulk of morbidity and symptoms are due to withdrawal from opioids, concomitant maternal use of other drugs associated with withdrawal symptoms is common. These exposures typically will worsen NAS symptoms and duration, but exposures are difficult to quantify in practice and ultimately do not impact management decisions. Others, including the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), advocate the use of the term “neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome” (NOWS) to more specifically link symptoms to opioid exposure.6 For the purposes of this review, the more commonly and general term NAS will be used to implicitly describe withdrawal symptoms driven primarily by in utero opioid exposure. Physician prescription of opioids occurs in 14–37% of pregnancies,7 but the majority are for a short duration and not associated with neonatal withdrawal. Prolonged in utero exposure to opioids is requisite for a withdrawal syndrome, although a threshold exposure has not been established and maternal methadone dose is only weakly associated with neonatal symptoms.8 Cardinal manifestations of neonatal opioid withdrawal are grouped into central nervous system (CNS), autonomic, and gastrointestinal domains. Seizures are of greatest concern, but are uncommon in the current era of earlier recognition and treatment. NAS symptoms have clinical impact mainly on feeding, with attendant negative effects on growth and development. Nonpharmacologic treatments should be used in all infants with in utero exposure to opioids. There is no universal definition of what constitutes a nonpharmacologic treatment, but common measures include the infant rooming with the mother,9 encouraging breast feeding,10 multiple small feedings, swaddling,11 and minimization of stimuli. Conceptually, all infants should be considered to be along a spectrum of symptom severity. Even with nonpharmacological interventions, over half of infants with signs of withdrawal will require pharmacologic treatment. CURRENT PHARMACOLOGIC APPROACHES TO NAS The need for pharmacologic treatment, and titration of dose, is guided by a symptom score. The Finnegan scoring instrument12 is the most widely used, but local variations are common. The MOTHER NAS score,13 a modification of the Finnegan instrument, is standardized and is the most commonly reported in clinical trials. An opioid is the primary therapy,14 using a strategy of titrating doses to control symptoms and slowly weaning down. Morphine is used at 80% of centers in the US, with methadone being used in the remainder.15 Phenobarbital or clonidine are used as adjunctive therapies in conjunction with an opioid when either maximum opioid dose has been reached, or in an initial coadministration with the goal of reducing opioid exposure. There is significant site-to-site heterogeneity in pharmacologic regimens, including starting and maximum dose, uptitration, and weaning parameters.16 There is a lack of definitive trials to guide therapy, although results of a multicenter trial comparing methadone and morphine (NCT01958476) will provide some guidance between these two drugs. There is similarly no consensus of the role of adjunctive therapy. Differing regimens involve the addition of clonidine or phenobarbital at maximum dose of opioid, the use of either agent in parallel with the opioid, or as an opioid-free monotherapy. Phenobarbital is a more nonspecific CNS depressant and is believed to be particularly useful in poly-substance exposures, although there are theoretical concerns about neurotoxicity.17 Clonidine has a mechanism more specific to opioid withdrawal and has a better evidence base of randomized trials, but it is used in less than 10% of hospitals treating NAS.15 IMPLICATIONS OF ADULT MEDICALLY ASSISTED THERAPY TO NEONATAL THERAPIES Methadone and buprenorphine are the two primary treatments for opioid use disorder. Short-acting opioids such as morphine are not used in adults as maintenance replacement. Clinical and dosing factors influencing buprenorphine effectiveness and treatment duration are shaped by route, regimen, infant characteristics, and adverse-event profiles. The evidence points to sublingual administration as the primary route, with the BBORN trial explicitly using sublingual buprenorphine and describing the solution as 0.075 mg per milliliter of simple syrup and 30% ethanol [N1-F2]. This route is also supported by the broader literature, which describes sublingual dosing as feasible in the neonatal population [N3-R2]. In contrast, the evidence does not strongly support intravenous or other routes in the provided sources, so any claims about those would be unsupported here.

Dosage regimens are central to effectiveness. The BBORN trial used a dose and regimen derived from efficacy, pharmacokinetic, and safety data generated in a phase 1 trial, and the article emphasizes that the dose was optimized for symptom control and weaning [N1-F2]. The broader literature similarly notes that pharmacometric modeling helps define exposure–response relationships and facilitates dose optimization [N3-F4]. The key takeaway is that dosing is not one-size-fits-all; it is adjusted based on infant response and pharmacokinetic data, with the trial explicitly using a single-site, randomized, double-blind, double-dummy design to compare sublingual buprenorphine with oral morphine [N1-F2].

Infant characteristics that predict response are only partially spelled out in the evidence. The BBORN trial reports that infants were randomized to receive either sublingual buprenorphine or oral morphine, and that the study included term infants exposed to opioids in utero with signs of neonatal abstinence syndrome [N1-F2]. It also notes that the study excluded infants with major congenital malformations, birth weight <2200 g, serious medical or neurologic illness, and other exclusions [N1-F2]. These exclusions suggest that effectiveness may depend on gestational age, weight, and comorbid burden, but the provided evidence does not give a detailed list of predictor variables such as birth weight, maternal opioid type, or severity of withdrawal. The broader literature does indicate that maternal methadone dose is only weakly associated with neonatal symptoms and that the threshold exposure is not established [N3-F4], which implies that infant response is influenced by more than just maternal dosing alone.

Adverse events and discontinuation reasons are reported in the BBORN trial as similar between groups, with no significant difference in adverse-event rates [N1-F2]. The study also notes that adjunctive phenobarbital was administered in 15% of the buprenorphine group and 23% of the morphine group, but this difference was not statistically significant [N1-F2]. The broader literature similarly states that buprenorphine has a wide therapeutic index for respiratory depression and a long half-life, which may make it useful for treatment [N1-F2], while the consensus guidelines emphasize that nonpharmacologic interventions are important and that pharmacologic treatment is used when symptoms are not controlled by behavioral approaches [N1-F1]. This suggests that discontinuation can occur either because symptoms remain uncontrolled or because adjunctive therapy is added, but the provided evidence does not provide a detailed breakdown of discontinuation reasons beyond phenobarbital use.

Overall, the evidence base here supports a model in which effectiveness and duration depend on sublingual route, optimized dosing, infant-specific exclusions and comorbidities, and careful monitoring for adverse events [N1-F2][N3-R2][N3-F4]. The main gap is that the sources do not provide a comprehensive list of infant predictors or a detailed long-term discontinuation analysis, so conclusions about individual-level predictors remain limited [N1-F2].

Buprenorphine in NOWS is most commonly compared with morphine, with the evidence base also including methadone and adjunctive treatments such as phenobarbital or clonidine. The most directly relevant study is the BBORN trial, which randomized term infants exposed to opioids in utero and with signs of neonatal abstinence syndrome to receive sublingual buprenorphine or oral morphine [N1-F2]. The trial also excluded infants who required adjunctive treatment beyond the primary opioid, but the provided evidence shows that adjunctive phenobarbital was used in both groups [N1-F2]. The broader literature similarly states that methadone is used in some centers, while morphine is used at 80% of centers in the US, and that clonidine is used as an adjunctive therapy [N1-F1][N3-F4].

Treatment allocation was randomized in the BBORN trial, with infants assigned in a 1:1 ratio to either sublingual buprenorphine or oral morphine [N1-F2]. The trial was double-blind and double-dummy, meaning that neither infants nor caregivers could reliably distinguish the treatments, and the study was blinded to the drug assignment [N1-F2]. The provided evidence also notes that randomization was stratified by maternal exposure to methadone or buprenorphine and by maternal intention to breast-feed or bottle-feed [N1-F2], which strengthens internal validity by reducing confounding between treatment groups. The broader literature further indicates that there is significant site-to-site heterogeneity in pharmacologic regimens, including starting and maximum dose, uptitration, and weaning parameters [N1-F1], suggesting that trial design varies in real-world practice.

Effectiveness differences observed between groups were substantial. In the BBORN trial, the median duration of treatment was significantly shorter with buprenorphine than with morphine: 15 days vs. 28 days [N1-F2]. The median length of hospital stay was also shorter with buprenorphine: 21 days vs. 33 days [N1-F2]. The trial also found that adjunctive phenobarbital use was less common in the buprenorphine group than in the morphine group, though the difference was not statistically significant [N1-F2]. The broader literature corroborates this by noting that clonidine and buprenorphine demonstrated superior safety profiles and shorter treatment duration compared to morphine in controlling NOWS [N1-F1]. Additional evidence from a single-center study states that buprenorphine was associated with shorter lengths of treatment and hospital stay compared to the comparator treatment [N3-R3]. This pattern across sources supports the conclusion that buprenorphine generally outperforms morphine in reducing treatment duration, with some evidence suggesting possible advantages over methadone and clonidine as adjuncts [N1-F1][N3-R3].

The comparator landscape is therefore broad: the main direct comparator in the provided evidence is morphine, with methadone and clonidine also appearing as relevant comparisons in the broader literature [N1-F1][N3-R3]. Blinding and randomization are well established in the BBORN trial, but the evidence does not provide a comparable level of detail for methadone or clonidine studies, so those comparisons should be interpreted cautiously [N1-F2].

Clinical studies assessing effectiveness in NOWS use a mix of randomized trials and observational designs, with the evidence base here leaning heavily on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and systematic review/explanatory synthesis designs. The BBORN trial is the most informative direct RCT, described as a single-site, double-blind, double-dummy clinical trial [N1-F2]. The broader literature also mentions a multicenter trial comparing methadone and morphine (NCT01958476), which is relevant as an example of a larger, multi-center trial design [N1-F1]. In addition, the evidence includes a systematic review that could not be converted into a meta-analysis because of heterogeneity across study designs and outcomes [N1-F1]. This indicates that observational and heterogeneous trial designs also contribute to the evidence base, but the quality of those designs is lower than the standardized RCT evidence.

Primary and secondary outcomes measured in NOWS studies are centered on symptom control, duration of treatment, and safety. The BBORN trial’s primary end point was the duration of treatment for symptoms of neonatal opioid withdrawal [N1-F2]. Secondary clinical end points included the length of hospital stay, the percentage of infants who required supplemental treatment with phenobarbital, and safety [N1-F2]. The broader literature similarly reports that buprenorphine was associated with shorter lengths of treatment and hospital stay compared to morphine [N3-R3], and that clonidine and buprenorphine demonstrated shorter treatment duration compared to morphine [N1-F1]. A separate source also reports that symptom-based dosing shortened hospital stay in neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome [N2-R3], and that a study demonstrated reduced total drug exposure and length of stay while successfully completing acute withdrawal [N2-R5]. These outcomes suggest that effectiveness is measured not only by treatment duration but also by medication exposure, safety, and discharge readiness.

Operationalizing treatment duration and withdrawal severity is a key issue. The BBORN trial operationalized treatment duration as the time until symptoms were controlled and treatment could be discontinued [N1-F2]. The trial also used the MOTHER NAS score, a modified Finnegan scoring instrument, as the main measure of withdrawal severity [N1-F2]. The evidence further indicates that treatment duration is often reported as a median or mean, with the BBORN trial explicitly stating a median duration of 15 days for buprenorphine and 28 days for morphine [N1-F2]. The broader literature also reports median duration of treatment and median length of hospital stay, and it notes that the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends up to 7 days of observation in some settings [N6-R3]. This suggests that withdrawal severity is operationalized through symptom scores, and treatment duration is reported as a central tendency metric rather than as a single fixed cutoff.

The evidence therefore supports a model in which effectiveness is assessed through randomized trials with symptom-based outcomes, and through observational or comparative studies that look at duration, hospital stay, medication exposure, and safety [N1-F1][N1-F2][N2-R3][N2-R5]. The main limitations of the evidence base are heterogeneity across study designs and the lack of standardized outcome reporting [N1-F1].

The evidence base for buprenorphine in NOWS has several important limitations and gaps. First, study limitations include heterogeneity across study designs and outcomes, which prevented a meta-analysis in the systematic review cited in the evidence [N1-F1]. This heterogeneity implies that direct comparisons across trials are not straightforward, and that the strength of evidence is lower than in a highly homogeneous RCT setting. The BBORN trial itself is a single-site study, which is a strength in terms of control but also a limitation in terms of generalizability [N1-F2]. The broader literature also notes that there is significant site-to-site heterogeneity in pharmacologic regimens, including starting and maximum dose, uptitration, and weaning parameters [N1-F1], which further complicates comparison.

Missing data on long-term follow-up or relapse are another gap. The provided evidence focuses almost entirely on acute treatment outcomes such as duration of treatment, hospital stay, and safety during the neonatal hospitalization [N1-F2][N2-R3][N2-R5]. There is no direct evidence in the sources cited here about long-term follow-up, relapse, or long-term developmental outcomes. The BBORN trial does not mention follow-up after discharge, and the systematic review does not report long-term outcomes either [N1-F1]. This means that current evidence is insufficient to assess whether buprenorphine reduces long-term opioid use, relapse, or adverse developmental outcomes.

Generalizability across populations and settings is limited. The BBORN trial included only term infants exposed to opioids in utero and excluded infants with major congenital malformations, birth weight <2200 g, serious medical or neurologic illness, and other exclusions [N1-F2]. This makes the findings most relevant to a relatively homogeneous group of term infants with opioid-exposed NOWS, but less directly applicable to preterm infants, infants with comorbid conditions, or different geographic settings. The broader literature also notes that prevalence and management vary widely by region, with increasing rates reported in Europe, Australia, and New Zealand, and with limited evidence in low- and middle-income countries [N1-F1]. This regional variation suggests that findings may not generalize equally across settings, especially where opioid prescribing practices and health systems differ.

Finally, the evidence base is still relatively limited in quantity and quality. The systematic review explicitly states that no meta-analysis was feasible due to heterogeneity, and that the review included 28 publications [N1-F1]. This implies that the field is growing but remains fragmented, with insufficient standardized reporting to support strong consensus. The provided evidence also highlights that there is no universal definition of what constitutes a nonpharmacologic treatment, and that outcomes such as length of stay and hospital stay can be influenced by systems-level interventions such as symptom-based dosing or clinical pathways [N1-F1][N2-R3]. These factors mean that observed differences in treatment duration may partly reflect intervention design rather than a single pharmacologic effect.

Overall, the evidence is strongest for acute treatment outcomes in a controlled trial setting, but weaker for long-term follow-up, relapse, and broad generalizability [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The main gaps are heterogeneity, limited long-term data, and variable applicability across populations and settings [N1-F1][N1-F2].

Treatment duration in NOWS is defined and reported through several overlapping metrics, with the most consistent operationalizations being days in hospital, days on medication, and days until discharge. The BBORN trial operationalized duration of treatment as the time until symptoms were controlled and treatment could be discontinued [N1-F2]. It also reported the median duration of treatment and the median length of hospital stay as primary outcomes, with values of 15 days vs. 28 days and 21 days vs. 33 days, respectively [N1-F2]. This indicates that duration is often reported as a central tendency measure rather than a fixed cutoff. A separate source notes that the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends up to 7 days of observation in some infants with chronic opioid exposure, but this is not a universal standard [N6-R3]. Another source reports a benchmark treatment duration of 2 to 4 weeks, with all infants being medication-free at least 48 hours before discharge [N6-R4]. These different benchmarks suggest that duration can be operationalized in relation to both symptom control and discharge readiness.

Duration is also reported as a discontinuation criterion. The BBORN trial explicitly uses discontinuation of treatment as the endpoint, meaning that duration is tied to when treatment can be safely stopped [N1-F2]. A related source notes that weaning represents the longest time interval of drug treatment and that stopping medications too early may not completely treat NOWS symptoms [N6-R2]. This means that duration is not only a measure of time in treatment but also a clinical decision point based on symptom resolution. The study on symptom-based dosing reports that infants were ready for discharge about 2.3 days earlier than expected, with no adverse effects reported [N2-R3]. This further supports the idea that duration is often reported relative to expected or target discharge readiness.

The evidence also indicates that duration is reported as median, mean, or discontinuation criteria. The BBORN trial reports median duration of treatment and median length of hospital stay [N1-F2], while the broader literature includes reports of median and mean duration in other studies [N1-R4]. The systematic review and meta-analysis background also highlights that length of stay is a critical metric influenced by systems-led strategies, but the provided evidence here does not provide enough detail to judge whether all studies consistently use the same statistical reporting method [N5-R3]. The evidence is therefore best summarized as reporting duration through median or mean values, with discontinuation criteria tied to treatment cessation and discharge.

Missing or censored data are handled in the provided evidence by reporting only completed treatment outcomes and by using blinded, randomized designs that reduce bias. The BBORN trial is double-blind, double-dummy, and randomized, which helps minimize missing data due to loss of follow-up [N1-F2]. The source on symptom-based dosing states that infants who were ready for discharge were compared to expected discharge timing, suggesting that censored or missing data are handled by comparing observed readiness to expected timing rather than by imputing missing values [N2-R3]. The broader evidence does not provide detailed information on imputation methods, so that limitation is not fully quantified in the provided sources. Overall, the evidence suggests that duration is reported as a central tendency measure and as a discontinuation criterion, with missing data handled primarily through randomized trial design and observed readiness to discharge [N1-F2][N2-R3][N6-R4].

Clinical studies assessing the effectiveness of buprenorphine in neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome (NOWS) focus on reducing treatment duration through a combination of randomized trials, observational studies, and comparative analyses. The evidence base is strongest for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and a systematic review that highlights heterogeneity across study designs and outcomes [N1-F1][N1-F2]. In addition to RCTs, the evidence includes observational and comparative studies that examine length of hospital stay, medication exposure, safety, and discharge readiness [N1-F1][N2-R3][N2-R5]. Overall, effectiveness is assessed not only by whether symptoms improve but also by how quickly treatment can be discontinued and how quickly infants can be discharged.

## 1) Study designs used to assess effectiveness
The clinical evidence is dominated by randomized trials. The BBORN trial is the most directly relevant example: it was a single-site, double-blind, double-dummy clinical trial comparing sublingual buprenorphine with oral morphine in term infants exposed to opioids in utero and with signs of neonatal abstinence syndrome [N1-F2]. This design is important because it uses randomization and blinding to reduce bias, making it the gold standard for assessing comparative effectiveness [N1-F2].

The evidence also includes a multicenter trial comparing methadone and morphine, which is relevant for understanding the broader comparator landscape and the heterogeneity of trial designs in NOWS [N1-F1]. In addition, the systematic review notes that no meta-analysis was feasible due to heterogeneity across study designs and outcomes, indicating that observational studies and heterogeneous trial designs also contribute to the evidence base, though with less rigor than standardized RCTs [N1-F1].

## 2) Primary and secondary outcomes measured
Clinical studies in NOWS typically use a mix of primary and secondary outcomes. The BBORN trial’s primary endpoint was the duration of treatment for symptoms of neonatal opioid withdrawal [N1-F2]. Its secondary clinical endpoints included the length of hospital stay, the percentage of infants requiring supplemental treatment with phenobarbital, and safety [N1-F2]. These outcomes reflect a practical approach to assessing effectiveness: not only whether symptoms improve, but also how long treatment lasts, how long the infant stays in the hospital, and whether adjunctive therapy is needed [N1-F2].

Other studies in the evidence base also use related outcomes. A related source notes that weaning represents the longest time interval of drug treatment and that stopping medications too early may not completely treat NOWS symptoms [N6-R2]. This means that duration is not only a measure of time in treatment but also a clinical decision point based on symptom resolution. Another source reports that infants were ready for discharge about 2.3 days earlier than expected, with no adverse effects reported [N2-R3]. This further supports the idea that duration is often reported relative to expected or target discharge readiness [N2-R3].

Duration is also reported as median, mean, or discontinuation criteria. The BBORN trial reports median duration of treatment and median length of hospital stay [N1-F2]. The broader literature includes reports of median and mean duration in other studies [N1-R4]. The evidence also notes that the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends up to 7 days of observation in some infants with chronic opioid exposure, but this is not a universal standard [N6-R3]. A separate source reports a benchmark treatment duration of 2 to 4 weeks, with all infants being medication-free at least 48 hours before discharge [N6-R4]. These different benchmarks suggest that duration can be operationalized in relation to both symptom control and discharge readiness [N6-R3][N6-R4].

Missing or censored data are handled in the provided evidence by reporting only completed treatment outcomes and by using blinded, randomized designs that reduce bias. The BBORN trial is double-blind, double-dummy, and randomized, which helps minimize missing data due to loss of follow-up [N1-F2]. The source on symptom-based dosing states that infants who were ready for discharge were compared to expected discharge timing, suggesting that censored or missing data are handled by comparing observed readiness to expected timing rather than by imputing missing values [N2-R3]. The broader evidence does not provide detailed information on imputation methods, so that limitation is not fully quantified in the provided sources. Overall, the evidence suggests that duration is reported as a central tendency measure and as a discontinuation criterion, with missing data handled primarily through randomized trial design and observed readiness to discharge [N1-F2][N2-R3][N6-R4].

## 7) Limitations and gaps in the evidence base
The evidence base has several important limitations. First, study limitations include heterogeneity across study designs and outcomes, which prevented a meta-analysis in the systematic review [N1-F1]. This heterogeneity implies that direct comparisons across trials are not straightforward, and that the strength of evidence is lower than in a highly homogeneous RCT setting. The BBORN trial itself is a single-site study, which is a strength in terms of control but also a limitation in terms of generalizability [N1-F2]. The broader literature also notes that there is significant site-to-site heterogeneity in pharmacologic regimens, including starting and maximum dose, uptitration, and weaning parameters [N1-F1], which further complicates comparison.

Missing data on long-term follow-up or relapse are another gap. The provided evidence focuses almost entirely on acute treatment outcomes such as duration of treatment, hospital stay, and safety during the neonatal hospitalization [N1-F2][N2-R3][N2-R5]. There is no direct evidence in the sources cited here about long-term follow-up, relapse, or long-term developmental outcomes. The BBORN trial does not mention follow-up after discharge, and the systematic review does not report long-term outcomes either [N1-F1]. This means that current evidence is insufficient to assess whether buprenorphine reduces long-term opioid use, relapse, or adverse developmental outcomes.

Generalizability across populations and settings is limited. The BBORN trial included only term infants exposed to opioids in utero and excluded infants with major congenital malformations, birth weight <2200 g, serious medical or neurologic illness, and other exclusions [N1-F2]. This makes the findings most relevant to a relatively homogeneous group of term infants with opioid-exposed NOWS, but less directly applicable to preterm infants, infants with comorbid conditions, or different geographic settings. The broader literature also notes that prevalence and management vary widely by region, with increasing rates reported in Europe, Australia, and New Zealand, and with limited evidence in low- and middle-income countries [N1-F1]. This regional variation suggests that findings may not generalize equally across settings, especially where opioid prescribing practices and health systems differ.

Finally, the evidence base is still relatively limited in quantity and quality. The systematic review explicitly states that no meta-analysis was feasible due to heterogeneity, and that the review included 28 publications [N1-F1]. This implies that the field is growing but remains fragmented, with insufficient standardized reporting to support strong consensus. The provided evidence also highlights that there is no universal definition of what constitutes a nonpharmacologic treatment, and that outcomes such as length of stay and hospital stay can be influenced by systems-level interventions such as symptom-based dosing or clinical pathways [N1-F1][N2-R3]. These factors mean that observed differences in treatment duration may partly reflect intervention design rather than a single pharmacologic effect.

## 8) Bottom line
Clinical studies assess buprenorphine effectiveness in NOWS by comparing it with morphine, methadone, and adjunctive treatments in randomized trials and observational studies. They measure effectiveness through duration of treatment, length of hospital stay, medication exposure, safety, and readiness for discharge. Buprenorphine is most often reported as reducing treatment duration and hospital stay, with the BBORN trial showing median treatment durations of 15 days versus 28 days for buprenorphine versus morphine [N1-F2]. However, the evidence is strongest in acute, controlled settings and weaker for long-term follow-up, relapse, and broad generalizability [N1-F1][N1-F2]. Overall, the studies suggest that buprenorphine may shorten NOWS treatment duration, but the evidence is still limited by heterogeneity, missing long-term data, and variable applicability across populations and settings [N1-F1][N1-F2].
